4. Short point for consideration is whether action taken by the management against Manoj Kumar Nunia in 
dismissing him from service of the company is legal and justified? If not, what relief the workman is entitled to? 


5. Both parties adduced evidence in this case. Manoj Kumar Nunia filed an affidavit-in-chief where he 
reiterated his case disclosed in the written statement. Objection raised by the workman is that he was absent due to his 
illness which was beyond his control and enquiry was held without providing him opportunity to defend his case as 
medical certificates were ignored by the Enquiry Officer. He further stated that he had also submitted death certificate 
of his sister which was one of the reasons for his absence from duty. Manoj Kumar Nunia examined himself as 
Workman Witness-I and he produced the following documents: 


(i) copy of charge sheet issued to the workman due to his absence is marked as Exhibit W-1. 
(ii) copy of enquiry proceeding in five pages is collectively marked as Exhibit W-2. 


(iii) copy of application dated 09/12/2019 whereby the workman along with his family members had prayed for 
allowing him to join duty is marked as Exhibit W-3. 


(iv) copy of another application submitted by the workman along with his family members requesting the 
management to allow him to join duty is marked as Exhibit W-4. 


(५) copy of application dated 04/04/2022 for allowing the workman to join duty is marked as Exhibit W-5. 


During cross-examination workman witness admitted that he received second show cause Notice at his home 
address before his dismissal from service. Workman further admitted that in the year 2015 he attended duty for only 
six days, in the year 2014 he was absent throughout the year and in the year 2013 he attended duty for twelve days 
only. Witness deposed that he informed that Enquiry Officer that due to illness of his sister he was unable to attend 
duty. It transpires from the testimony of workman witness that he did not submit application informing the 
management about his illness nor did he take any prior permission for his absence from duty. 


6. Mr. Sumanta Bhattacharya is examined as Management Witness-I. He filed an affidavit-in-chief reaffirming 
the statements made in written statement of the management. Witness further stated that since misconduct of the 
workman was serious and grave in nature, management decided to dismiss the workman from service. Management 
issued a second show cause Notice to the workman but he failed to submit reply against findings of the Enquiry 
Officer. Witness further averred that management is justified in dismissing the workman from service and he is not 
entitled to any relief of reinstatement or back wages. In course of examination, witness produced the following 
documents: 


(i) Copy of charge sheet dated 21/04/2016 by which charges under clause 26.29 for absenting from duties 
beyond ten days without sanction leave, under clause 26.5 for willful neglect of work, under clause 26.22 for 
sabotage or causing willful damage to work in progress or to property of the company and under cause 26.23 
for habitual late attendance or habitual absence from duty without sufficient cause were levelled against him 
is marked as Exhibit M-1 


(ii) Copy of office order dated 20/21.05.2016 by which Ravi Bara, Asst. Manager (P) was appointed as the 
Enquiry Officer is marked as Exhibit M-2. 


(iii) Copy of application submitted by Manoj Kumar Nunia seeking time for attending the enquiry proceeding is 
marked as Exhibit M-3. 


(iv) Copy of enquiry proceeding in four pages is collectively marked as Exhibit M-4. 
(५) Copy of enquiry report dated 01/06/2017 is marked as Exhibit M-5. 
(vi) Copy of second show cause Notice is marked as Exhibit M-6. 


(vii) Copy of order of dismissal dated 05/14.10.2017 issued by the General Manager, Sodepur Area, whereby he 
was dismissed from service for his misconduct is marked as Exhibit M-7. 


(viii) | Copy of Note sheet dated 02/03.06.2017 proposing termination of service of the workman in two pages is 
collectively marked as Exhibit M-8. 


In cross-examination Management witness deposed that the Enquiry Officer extended opportunity to the 
charged workman for engaging co-workers to assist him in the enquiry. He stated that after dismissal from service, 
workman submitted three mercy petitions praying for his reinstatement in his service. Dismissed workman was not 
informed about finality of mercy petitions submitted by him. He also denied suggestion that punishment of dismissal 
from service of the workman was disproportionate to the nature of misconduct. 


7. Mr. Rakesh Kumar, union representative, arguing the case on behalf of the dismissed workman submitted 
that the alleged unauthorized absence of the workman was for a period of four months and twenty two days only. The 
Workman participated in the enquiry proceeding and produced documents in support of his illness but the

management without providing proper opportunity to represent his case dismissed the workman from service. Union 
representative argued that nature of punishment is also disproportionate to the nature of misconduct mentioned in the 
charge sheet, which is absence for less than five months. Union representative accordingly prayed for setting aside the 
order of dismissal passed against Manoj Kumar Nunia and for his reinstatement in service along with back wages. 


8. Mr. P. K. Das, learned advocate in reply argued that the workman had burdened the management by his 
habitual absence from duty and his attendance in the previous three years was poor. Workman was given several 
opportunities but he did not amend his conduct and continued to remain absent without any information and seeking 
prior permission from the management. He submitted that contradictory reasons were cited by the workman for his 
unauthorized absence from duty. After receiving charge sheet, he submitted an application dated 21/03/2017 
addressed to the Asst. Manager (P) seeking time for enquiry on the ground that due to physical problem he could not 
attend enquiry on 23/08/2016. During his participation in the enquiry, no document was submitted to prove that he 
was suffering from illness. Ld. Advocate strenuously argued that workman willfully neglected his duty in a habitual 
manner and the management found him guilty of charge under clauses 26.23 and 26.29 of the Certified Standing 
Order. All possible measures were taken and the principle of Natural Justice was followed at the time of enquiry. The 
Disciplinary Authority issued a second show cause Notice to the workman dated 09/14.06.2017 (Exhibit M-6) 
seeking his explanation or reply within fifteen days. Workman initially denied that he received second show cause 
Notice but, in the cross-examination admitted that he received second show cause Notice. No reply was submitted by 
the workman to deny the findings against him. Management did not find extenuating circumstances in the conduct of 
the workman to take a liberal view or impose a lighter punishment. It is argued that decision taken by the 
management is appropriate and the workman is not entitled to any relief. 


9. I have considered the argument advanced on behalf of the workman and the management in light of the 
Industrial Dispute raised, attending facts and circumstances of the case derived from pleading and evidence on record. 
Workman was admittedly absent from 28/11/2015 to 20/04/2016. He did not inform the management that he was 
unable to attend duty for any plausible reason nor did he take prior permission from the employer company. 
Management therefore was in dark about attendance of the workman. After a passage of more than four months of 
absence, a charge sheet was issued to him disclosing the charges of unauthorized absence from duty beyond ten days, 
habitual absence from duty without sufficient cause, willful neglect of work and sabotage or causing willful damage 
to work in progress or to property of the company. Workman did not care to submit reply to the charge sheet. He 
turned up on 21/03/2017 and sought for time to attend the enquiry. Enquiry Officer extended reasonable opportunity 
to the charged workman to participate in the proceeding and defend himself against the arraignment. Statement of 
Manoj Kumar Nunia was recorded after the management witnesses were examined in support of the charge. During 
enquiry, workman stated that he absented from duty due to his sister’s illness who was admitted in Mission Hospital, 
Durgapur, with some incurable disease and she died on 25/05/2016. He went further stating before the Enquiry officer 
that he was mentally disturbed for problems in his family. In cross-examination, charged employee was asked 
whether he informed the Unit Management about his absence or illness to which he replied in the negative. He was 
categorically questioned if he can show prescription made by the Doctor to which the workman also answered in the 
negative. From the materials in enquiry proceeding, it appears that the workman never claimed to be suffering from 
illness nor did he produce medical documents before the Enquiry officer. I find from the record that the Enquiry 
Officer in course of the enquiry proceeding observed the principle of Natural Justice and arrived at a finding on the 
basis of statements made before him. Claim by the workman in written statement that he was suffering from illness 
and produced medical documents are outcome of afterthought. Cross-examination of WW-I reveals that his past 
attendance was extremely poor. Therefore, the findings of the Enquiry Officer against the workman appears consistent 
with the fact and circumstances which have been established against the workman through evidence. Enquiry Officer 
in his finding dated 01/06/2017 (Exhibit M-5) observed that Manoj Kumar Nunia failed to produce medical 
prescription or cash memo of purchase of medicines during the period of his absence. The Enquiry Officer concluded 
that charge levelled under clauses 26.23 and 26.29 of Certified Standing Order stood proved beyond doubt. General 
Manager, Sodepur Area in a fair manner provided second opportunity to the workman for his explanation regarding 
finding made against him. Second show cause Notice dated 09/14.06.2017 has been produced as Exhibit M-6. 
Workman in a nonchalant manner during his examination denied receiving second show cause Notice for gaining 
some sympathy in his favour. However, contrary to his earlier statement admitted in the cross-examination that 
second show cause Notice was served upon him but the workman did not reply to the same. Therefore, the 
Disciplinary Authority after considering all materials and previous attendance of the workman dismissed him from 
service. Order of dismissal was communicated to Manoj Kumar Nunia under registered post with AD (Exhibit M-7). 
It is true that dismissed workman thereafter made attempts to regain his employment by submitting mercy petitions on 
09/12/2019, 04/03/2020 and 04/04/2022 (Exhibits W-3, W-4 and W-5 respectively). Even this approach of the 
workman lacked promptitude as he came up with mercy petitions after two years from his dismissal on 14/10/2017. In 
my considered view, charge has been well established against the workman through a proper enquiry. There is no 
mitigating circumstance in favour of the workman for his reinstatement in service by casting aside his continuous 
misconduct of unauthorized and habitual absence. Punishment awarded against the workman arising out of domestic 
enquiry appears to be just, proportionate and legally tenable. The dismissed workman is not entitled to any relief in 
this case and the same is dismissed. 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : फरवरी 7, 2026/माध 18, 1947 691 


Hence, 
ORDERED 


that the Industrial Dispute is dismissed on contest against the workman. The dismissed workman is not entitled to any 
relief of reinstatement in service or back wages. Management of ECL is directed to make payment of any legal dues 
to the workman on account of his past service. Let an Award be drawn up in the light of my above discussion. Let 
copies of Award be communicated to the Ministry for information and Notification.

AWARD 


In exercise of powers conferred under clause (d) of Sub-section (1) and Sub-section (2A) of Section 10 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (14 of 1947), the Government of India through the Ministry of Labour, vide its Order 
No. L-22012/102/2013-IR(CM-II) dated 21/08/2013 has been pleased to refer the following dispute between the 
employer, that is the Management of Ghusick Colliery, Kalipahari (R) under Sripur Area of Eastern Coalfields 
Limited and their workman for adjudication by this Tribunal. 


“Whether the action of the management of Ghusick Colliery Kalipahari (R) under Sripur Area to dismiss 


692 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : FEBRUARY 7, 2026/MAGHA 18, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


from service to Sri Chhatrapati Majhi of Ghusick Colliery under Kalipahari (R) is fair, justified and 
proportionate punishment for absence from duty? If not so, what relief management can provide to him?” 


1. On receiving Order No. L-22012/102/2013-IR(CM-II) dated 21/08/2013 from the Government of India, 
Ministry of Labour, New Delhi for adjudication of the dispute, a Reference case No. 11 of 2013 was registered on 
14/02/2014 and an order was passed for issuing notice to the parties through registered post, directing them to appear 
and submit their written statements along with relevant documents in support of their claims. 


2. Mr. Rakesh Kumar, President, Koyala Mazdoor Congress filed written statement for the dismissed workman 
on 05/08/2014. In brief, fact of the case disclosed in the written statement of the union is that Chhatrapati Majhi was a 
permanent employee of ECL and was posted at Ghusick Colliery unit of Kalipahari (R) colliery under Sripur Area of 
ECL. He joined service on 26/10/1981 having U. Man No. 120909. Due to his illness, Chhatrapati Majhi could not 
attend his duty under ECL. After recovery from illness, he reported for joining duty but was neither allowed to join 
his duty nor did the management issue any order of dismissal against him. Workman waited for a long period and 
thereafter requested the union to take steps for his joining duty. Workman submitted a mercy petition before the 
management which was not considered. Thereafter, he raised an Industrial Dispute which ended in failure and the 
Ministry of Labour, Government of India referred the scheduled dispute before this Tribunal for adjudication. 
According to the workman, management should have issued charge sheet and should have conducted an enquiry as 
per the Certified Standing Order of the company. After holding enquiry, a decision could have been taken either to 
allow him to join duty or to punish him but the management without complying the essential prerequisites did not 
allow the workman to join his duty. According to the union, Chhatrapati Majhi has no employment and is unable to 
maintain his family. Union claimed that there is no fault on the part of Chhatrapati Majhi and he was forced to seat 
idle for the entire period. Union prayed for reinstatement of the workman in service along with full back wages and 
other consequential benefits. 


3. Management of Kalipahari Group of Mines, Sripur Area, ECL filed their written statement on 16/10/2023 
wherein it is stated that the instant dispute has been raised by the union over dismissal of Chhatrapati Majhi. 
According to the management, the ex-workman was charge sheeted for his unauthorized absence from duty but the 
workman failed to submit satisfactory reply to the charge sheet due to which a domestic enquiry was conducted by the 
Enquiry officer. Workman duly participated in the enquiry proceeding and he was given full opportunity to defend his 
case according to the principle of Natural Justice. The Enquiry Officer found Chhatrapati Majhi guilty of charge and 
submitted his enquiry report, enquiry proceeding and other relevant documents. Workman was dismissed from service 
on being found guilty of misconduct for unauthorized absence from duty. Management denied that enquiry 
proceeding was vitiated due to irregularities or that the punishment awarded to Chhatrapati Majhi was 
disproportionate. Management denied that the workman was unable to attend duty due to his illness. It is urged that 
fairness of enquiry is required to be decided as a preliminary issue and if the Tribunal found that the enquiry 
proceeding was unfair for any reason, management may be granted opportunity to prove the charge established 
against the workman by adducing further evidence. It is claimed that the action of the management in dismissing the 
workman is fully justified and he is not entitled to any relief. 


4. Short point for consideration in this reference is whether dismissal of Chhatrapati Majhi from service is fair 
and justified and if punishment awarded is proportionate to the misconduct of absence from duty? If not, what relief 
the dismissed workman is entitled to? 


5. After extending several opportunities management did not file any written statement and the case was fixed 
for evidence of workman witness on 26/09/2016. No evidence was adduced by the workman. On prayer of ECL, a 
belated written statement was filed after service of copy upon the union representative. Union did not adduce any 
evidence in favour of the workman witness. Finally, one Mr. Apurba Biswas was examined as Management Witness- 
I. In his affidavit-in-chief management witness, who was posted as Manager (P) at Kalipahari (R) Colliery, ECL 
stated that Chhatrapati Majhi was absent from duty from 11/07/1983 and was charge sheeted on 09/11/1983 under 
section 29(16) of Certified Standing Order of the company. Workman submitted reply to the charge sheet which was 
found unsatisfactory and a domestic enquiry was held in respect of the chargelevelled against the workman. Enquiry 
Officer issued Notice of Enquiry and after holding enquiry submitted his report. Workman did not participate in the 
enquiry proceeding to defend his case and the charge of misconduct was established against the workman. The 
Disciplinary Authority after careful consideration of the charge sheet, enquiry proceeding, enquiry report and all other 
connected papers issued order of dismissal of Chhatrapati Majhi from service vide letter dated 04/08.06.1984. 
According to the management, punishment was proportionate to the gravity of misconduct committed by the 
workman. Witness denied that the workman was prevented from his duty due to his illness. It is claimed that no 
intimation was given by the workman to the management for such unauthorized absence. Copies of enquiry 
proceeding and finding have been admitted in evidence. Following documents have been produced by the 
Management Witness-I: 


(i) Copy of charge sheet dated 09/11/1983 issued against Chhatrapati Majhi is marked as Exhibit M-1. 


(ii) Copy of reply submitted by the workman against the charge sheet, which appears as an explanatory note on 
the charge sheet is marked as Exhibit M-1/1. 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : फरवरी 7, 2026/माध 18, 1947 693 


(iii) Copy of letter of appointment of the Enquiry Officer dated 02/03/1984 is marked as Exhibit M-2. 


(iv) Copy of Notice of Enquiry dated 04/03/1984 which was issued by the Enquiry Officer and sent to 
Chhatrapati Majhi under registered post is marked as Exhibit M-3. 


(५) Xerox copy of postal envelope in which the Notice of Enquiry dated 04/03/1984 was sent to Chhatrapati 
Majhi at his address at Vill- Bhatta Para (Ningah) is marked as Exhibit M-4. 


(vi) Copy of enquiry proceeding is collectively marked as Exhibit M-5 and copy of finding of the enquiry is 
marked as Exhibit M-5/1. 


(vii) | Copy of letter dated 04/08.06.1984 issued by the General Manager addressed to Chhatrapati Majhi informing 
him that he has been dismissed from service with immediate effect is marked as Exhibit M-6. 


(viii) | Copy of letter issued by the management in respect of an application under RTI informing that Chhatrapati 
Majhi’s representation for reinstatement was not found fit for consideration since his age was not below forty five 
years, is marked as Exhibit M-7. 


In cross-examination, Management Witness deposed that Notice issued to the workman for enquiry was 
served upon him but he could not produce any document in support of such service. Management Witness denied that 
the workman was less than forty five years at the time of his dismissal or that the punishment imposed was 
disproportionate to the nature of charge established against him. 


6. Mr. Rakesh Kumar, union representative arguing the case on behalf of the dismissed workman submitted that 
the workman was suffering from illness due to which he was unable to attend duty. After recovery from illness when 
he reported for duty, he was not permitted to join and without issuing charge sheet and holding enquiry, workman has 
been held guilty of the charge of unauthorized absence and was dismissed from service. Mr. Kumar argued that due to 
absence from duty for three months and few days, the Disciplinary Authority has imposed a very harsh punishment, 
disproportionate to the alleged misconduct. He further argued that no second show cause Notice was issued to the 
workman and he was not given opportunity to get himself explained about the finding of the Enquiry Officer. 
Therefore, it is urged that order of dismissal issued against the workman is not sustainable and the order which is 
arbitrary and bad in law is liable to be set aside. It is asserted that the management should have considered the mercy 
petition submitted by the workman for his reinstatement in service and also pay the back wages to him for the period 
he was forced to remain idle. 


7. Mr. P. K. Das, learned advocate for the management of ECL refuting the argument advanced by the union 
representative submitted that in the instant case, workman who was appointed in service on 26/10/1981 as Trainee at 
Ghusick Colliery remained absent from service from 11/07/1983 without any intimation or authorization for the leave. 
Workman was issued charge sheet on 09/11/1983 levelling charge under section 29(16) of Certified Standing Order 
applicable to the company for his unauthorized absence causing dislocation of company’s work and inconvenience to 
fellow workmen. It is argued that charge sheet was served upon the workman and he submitted explanation on 
12/12/1983 denying that he was absent from 11/07/1983 and admitted that he was rather absent from 03/09/1983 due 
to jaundice and he was under medical treatment from 04/10/1983 to 11/12/1983. Ld. Advocate argued that 
unauthorized absence of the workman from service during trainee period speaks volumes against his misconduct and 
the management decided to hold a domestic enquiry against him for his unauthorized absence. A copy of charge sheet 
produced by the management is marked as Exhibit M-! and reply to the charge sheet by Chhatrapati Majhi is marked 
as Exhibit M-1/1. Referring to Exhibit M-2, a letter dated 29.02.1984/02.03.1984 issued by the Manager, Ghusick 
Colliery, submitted that Mr. Samir Kr. Banerjee was the Enquiry Officer to hold enquiry in respect of charge against 
Chhatrapati Majhi. Notice of enquiry (Exhibit M-3) was issued and sent to the workman at his address under 
registered post. Copy of postal envelope is produced as Exhibit M-4. Ld. Advocate for the management further argued 
that Notice of Enquiry was transmitted to the workman under registered post and a copy of Notice was displayed on 
the Notice Board of the office fixing 29/03/1984 as the date of enquiry. Since the workman did not participate, 
Enquiry Officer held ex-parte enquiry and examined management witnesses namely Mr. S. N. Laha, Timekeeper, 
New Ghusick Unit, Mr. Zanruj Khan, W.O.’s Clerk, New Ghusick Unit and Mr. B. K. Mojumder, Compounder, New 
Ghusick Medical Unit. Though charged workman in his reply stated that he was absent from 03/09/1983 and not from 
11/07/1983, all management witnesses consistently stated before the Enquiry Officer that the workman (Chhatrapati 
Majhi) was absent from duty from 11/07/1983 till date and he did not send information to the management that he 
was suffering from illness since 11/07/1983. Ld. Advocate for the management took me through the finding of the 
Enquiry Officer where the charged workman was found guilty of charge for unauthorized absence. Admittedly, no 
second show cause Notice was issued to the workman. At the relevant time there was no binding decision upon the 
management as was later laid down by Hon’ble Supreme Court in a case of Md. Ramzan Khan Vs. Government of 
India in 1993 that Second show cause Notice was mandatory. Ld. Advocate argued that ample opportunity was 
granted to the charged employee to defend his case and the principle of Natural Justice was duly followed by the 
Enquiry Officer. Charged employee being fully aware of issuance of charge sheet on 12/12/1983 did not bother to 
find out the consequence and preferred not to participate in the enquiry only to raise dispute at a later stage. It is 
argued that the Disciplinary Authority after considering all relevant materials, charge sheet, enquiry proceeding, 


694 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : FEBRUARY 7, 2026/MAGHA 18, 1947 [Part II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


report and evidence recorded by the Enquiry Officer, passed an order dismissing the workman from service with 
immediate effect i.e. 08/06/1984. Order of dismissal has been produced as Exhibit M-6. Ld. Advocate argued that 
punishment of dismissal is proportionate to the misconduct and the order of dismissal calls for no interference. 


8. I have considered the rival arguments advanced on behalf of the union and Id. Advocate for the management 
in the light of materials on record including pleading of parties, evidence and documents produced by the 
management as Exhibits. From evidence on record, it is well established that the aggrieved workman was appointed 
in service of the company on 26/10/1981 and it is admitted that without prior intimation or authorization of the 
management, he started absenting from duty. In the charge sheet, it is alleged that the workman absented from duty 
from 11/07/1983 whereas workman in his reply has stated that he was not absent from 11/07/1983 but failed to attend 
duty from 03/09/1983 duty due to jaundice and was under medical treatment from 04/10/1983 to 11/12/1983. 
Workman received charge sheet by putting signature on 12/12/1983 (Exhibit M-1) and he was fully aware of the 
charge of unauthorized absence levelled against him. Management of ECL not being satisfied with the explanation 
submitted by the workman against the charge decided to hold enquiry and appointed Enquiry Officer by letter dated 
02/03/1984 (Exhibit M-2). Enquiry Officer issued Notice of Enquiry on 04/03/1984 addressed to Chhatrapati Majhi 
fixing 29/03/1984 as date for enquiry and he was asked to appear at the office of the Welfare Officer at 10.30 a.m. 
along with a co-workman for assisting him. Notice of Enquiry was sent to Chhatrapati Majhi under registered post 
which was returned unserved with an endorsement “not known”. Enquiry Officer held ex-parte enquiry against 
Chhatrapati Majhi. Enquiry proceeding discloses that Notice under registered post was sent to the workman and the 
Notice was also displayed on the Notice Board before initiating enquiry proceeding. Three Management 
Representatives were examined who consistently stated that the workman was absent from 11/07/1983 till the date of 
enquiry on 29/03/1984, which continued thereafter. On a perusal of the enquiry proceeding (Exhibit M-5) and finding 
of the Enquiry Officer dated 31/03/1984 (Exhibit M-5/1) it appears to me that though enquiry was held only on one 
date, enquiry proceeding was held after giving sufficient opportunity to the charged workman who neither appeared 
nor sought for accommodation or adjournment of the proceeding to some other date. Mr. Rakesh Kumar, union 
representative submitted that the workman was unable to attend duty due to his illness but no document has been 
produced by the union in support of the cause of absence of the workman. It also appears from the enquiry proceeding 
during reference that the charged employee was not examined by the union to face cross-examination by the 
management. Therefore, contention of the workman that no opportunity was given to him before his dismissal is 
unacceptable. It is to be borne in mind that if a workman who joined service in October, 1981 resorts to unauthorized 
absence within a period of two years from the date of his employment in public sector would be a serious misconduct. 


9. Even if for argument sake it is accepted that the workman was actually suffering from illness which 
prevented him from duty, workman is still duty bound to inform the management of the company about the reasons 
for which he was unable to attend duty. By not informing the management about the reasons for his absence gives rise 
to a presumption that the workman has abandoned his work under the company and he is not entitled to any benefit. 
Hon’ble High Court of Punjab and Haryana in the case of Nav Bharat Industries Vs. Presiding Officer and 
another [2018 LLR 439], held that if a workman remained absent unauthorizedly for a long time, even due to his 
illness without informing the management about it, termination of his service by invoking conditions as stipulated in 
the Certified Standing Orders, is not illegal. It was further held that when the workman does not inform the 
management about his illness, remaining absent for a long time, presumption drawn by the management that the 
workman has abandoned his job of his own is justified. From the settled position of law, it would emerge that 
unauthorized absence compounded with non-communication of the reason of absence to the management are 
unacceptable and workman cannot derive any benefit of doubt. An illness cannot be ground for unauthorized absence 
and the workman would not be entitled to benefits. Workman in the instant case was dismissed from service in June, 
1984 and he raised Industrial Dispute before Government of India, Ministry of Labour only in the year 2013 i.e. after 
a lapse of twenty nine years. Prior to that, workman had filed application before the management for reinstatement on 
04/11/2009 and the application was not found fit for consideration as Chhatrapati Majhi was not less than forty five 
years of age which was a basic requirement for re-employment in terms of Memorandum of Settlement dated 
22/05/2007. In a case of Prabhakar Vs. Joint Director, Sericulture Department and Another [(2015) 15 SCC 1] 
it was laid down by the Hon’ble Court in Paragraph fourteen that “to summarize, although there is no limitation 
prescribed under the Act for making reference under Section 10 (1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, yet it is for the 
“appropriate government” to consider whether it is expedient or not to make the reference. The words “at any time” 
used in section 10(1) do not admit of any limitation in making an order of reference and laws of limitation are not 
applicable to proceedings under the Industrial Disputes Act. However, the policy of industrial adjudication is that 
very stale claim should not be generally encouraged or allowed in as much as unless there is satisfactory explanation 
for delay as, apart from obvious risk of industrial peace from the entertainment of claims after long lapse of time, it is 
necessary also to take into account the unsettling effect which it is likely to have on the employers financial 
arrangement and to avoid dislocation of an industry.” From the aforesaid decision it is pertinent to decide whether 
the Industrial Dispute raised by the union/workman is within a reasonable time from the cause of action or the same 
has been initiated after a very long period without explanation of delay. In the instant case, workman is absolutely 
oblivious about his disengagement since issuance of order of dismissal in June, 1984. After passage of more than 
twenty five years, workman sought for reinstatement in service and raised an Industrial Dispute after a period of 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : फरवरी 7, 2026/माध 18, 1947 695 


twenty nine years. There is no explanation as to why such inordinate delay occurred. Considering facts and 
circumstances of the case I hold that the Industrial Dispute raised by the workman has no merit in seeking relief. 
There is no cogent ground to explain long delay caused by the union in raising dispute. Therefore, I find no reason to 
interfere with the order of dismissal of the workman. 


Hence, 
ORDERED 
that the Industrial Dispute is dismissed on contest against Chhatrapati Majhi who is represented by Koyala Mazdoor 
Congress. Dismissed workman is not entitled to any relief in this case. Let an Award be drawn up in the light of my 


above discussion. Let copies of Award be communicated to the Ministry for information and Notification.

Som Prakash Rekhi v/s Union of India & Anr., (1981) 1 SCC 449, Held 

“In the present instance, the source of both, read in the light of Sections 3 and 7, is saturated with State 
functions. Avowedly, the statutory contemplation, as disclosed by Section 7, is that the Company should step 
into the shoes of the executive power of the State. The legislative milieu in which the second respondent came to 
be the successor of Burmah Shell suggests that the former is more than a mere company registered under the 
Companies Act. It has a statutory flavour acquired under Section 7. Moreover, everything about the second 
respondent in the matter of employees, their provident, superannuation and welfare funds, is regulated 
statutorily unlike in the case of ordinary companies. Sections 9 and 10 deal with these aspects. These two 
provisions which regulate the conditions of service and even provide for adjudication of disputes relating to

Sections 9 and 10, in terms, create rights and duties vis-a-vis the Government company itself apart from the 
Companies Act. An ordinary company, even a government company simpliciter has not the obligations cast on 
the second respondent by Sections 9 and 10. And, Section I1 specifically gives the Act primacy vis-a-vis other 
laws. Section 12, although it has no bearing on the specific dispute we are concerned with in this case, is a 
clear pointer to the statutory character of the Government company and the vesting of an authority therein. This 
provision clothes the Government company with power to take delivery of the property of Burmah Shell from

one in Section 12. The provision for penalties if any person meddles with the property of the second respondent 
emphasises the special character of this Government company. Equally unique is the protection conferred by 
Section 16 on the Government company and its officers and employees “for anything which is, in good faith,

Undertaking having vested in it by force of Section 7 of the Act. The various provisions to which our attention 
was drawn, an elaboration of which is not called for, emphasise the fact that the second respondent is not a

11. As far as acquittal of the appellant by a criminal court is concerned, in our opinion, the said order does not 
preclude the Corporation from taking an action if it is otherwise permissible. In our judgment, the law is fairly 
well settled. Acquittal by a criminal court would not debar an employer from exercising power in accordance 
with the Rules and Regulations in force. The two proceedings, criminal and departmental, are entirely different. 
They operate in different fields and have different objectives. Whereas the object of criminal trial is to inflict 
appropriate punishment on the offender, the purpose of enquiry proceedings is to deal with the delinquent 
departmentally and to impose penalty in accordance with the service rules. In a criminal trial, incriminating 
statement made by the accused in certain circumstances or before certain officers is totally inadmissible in 
evidence. Such strict rules of evidence and procedure would not apply to departmental proceedings. The degree 
of proof which is necessary to order a conviction is different from the degree of proof necessary to record the 
commission of delinquency. The rule relating to appreciation of evidence in the two proceedings is also not 
similar. In criminal law, burden of proof is on the prosecution and unless the prosecution is able to prove the 
guilt of the accused “beyond reasonable doubt”, he cannot be convicted by a court of law. In a departmental 
enquiry, on the other hand, penalty can be imposed on the delinquent officer on a finding recorded on the basis 
of “preponderance of probability”. Acquittal of the appellant by a Judicial Magistrate, therefore, does not ipso 
facto absolve him from the liability under the disciplinary jurisdiction of the Corporation. We are, therefore, 
unable to uphold the contention of the appellant that since he was acquitted by a criminal court, the impugned 
order dismissing him from service deserves to be quashed and set aside.

Dr. S.L. Agrawal v/s General Manager, Hindustan Steel, (1970) 1 SCC 177, (Five Judges Bench) Held 


“6. The question that arises in this case is: whether the employees of a Corporation such as the Hindustan Steel 
Ltd., are entitled to the protection of Article 311? This question can only be answered in favour of the appellant 
if we hold that the appellant held a civil post under the Union. It was conceded before us that the appellant 
could not be said to belong to the civil service of the Union or the State. Article 311, on which this contention is 
based, reads as follow: 


“311. Dismissal, removal, or reduction in rank of persons employed in civil capacities under the Union or a 
State.—(1) No person who is a member of a civil service of the Union or an all-India Service or a civil service 
of a State or holds a civil post under the Union or a State shall be dismissed or removed by an authority 
subordinate to that by which he was appointed. 


(2) No such person as aforesaid shall be dismissed or removed or reduced in rank until he has been given a 
reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him: 


Provided that this clause shall not apply— 


(a) where a person is dismissed or removed or reduced in rank on the ground of conduct which has led to his 
conviction on a criminal charge; 


(b) where an authority empowered to dismiss or remove a person or to reduce him in rank is satisfied that for 
some reasons, to be recorded by that authority in writing, it is not reasonably practicable to give to that person 
an opportunity of showing cause; or 


(c) where the President or Governor, as the case may be, is satisfied that in the interest of security of the State it 
is not expedient to give to that person such an opportunity. 


(3) If any question arises whether it is reasonably practicable to give to any person an opportunity of showing 
cause under clause (2), the decision thereon of the authority empowered to dismiss or remove such person or to 
reduce him in rank, as the case may be, shall be final.” 


7. Clause (2) of the article, which gives the protection opens with the words “no such person as aforesaid” and 
these words take one back to clause(1) which describes the person or persons to whom the protection is 
intended to go. Clause (1) speaks of (i) persons who are members of (a) a Civil Service of the Union, or (b) an 
all-India Service or (c) a Civil Service of a State or (ii) hold a civil post under the Union or a State. (a), (b) and 
(c) refer to the standing services which have been created in the Union and the States and which are 
permanently maintained in strength. In addition to the standing services there are certain posts which are 
outside the permanent services. The last category in Article 311(1) therefore speaks of such posts on the civil 
side as opposed to the military side. Incumbents of such posts also receive protection. 


6. In the present case the appellant did not belong to any of the permanent services. He held a post which was 
not borne on any of the standing services. It was, however, a civil post as opposed to a military post. So far the 
appellant's case is clear but the clause speaks further that such posts must be under the Union or a State. The 
question thus is whether the servant employed here can be said to have held the post under the Union or a 
State? The appellant contends that since Hindustan Steel Limited is entirely financed by the Government and its 
management is directly the responsibility of the President, the post is virtually under the Government of India. 


9. This argument ignores some fundamental concepts in relation to incorporated companies. In support of the 
contention that the post must be regarded as one under the Union the appellant relies on some obiter 
observations of a Single Judge in M. Verghese v. Union of India [AIR 1963 Cal 421] . In that case the 
petitioners were drivers working for the Durgapur Project under Hindustan Steel Limited. The learned Single 
Judge considered the question by analysing the set up of Hindustan Steel Limited. He found that it was a 
Government company and a private limited company, although it did not include in its name any notice that it 
was a private company. He referred in detail to the various provisions in the Articles of Association as also in 
the Indian Companies Act which rendered the ordinary company law inapplicable in certain respects and 
conferred unlimited powers of management on the President of India and his nominees. He also found that 
Hindustan Steel Limited was entirely owned by the Union of India. From this the learned Judge wished to infer 
that Hindustan Steel Limited was really a department of the Government but he did not express this opinion and

support of a decision reported in Ram Babu Rathaur v. Divisional Manager, Life Insurance Corporation of 
India [AIR 1961 All 502] and another in Damodar Valley Corporation v. Provat Roy. [LX CWN 1023] Our 
brother Ramaswami relied in particular upon an English case Tamlin v. Hennaford [(1950) I KBD 18] . In that 
case it was held in relation to a business that although the minister was really incharge, the corporation was 
different from the Crown and the services of the corporation were not civil services. Justice P.B. Mukherjee of 
the Calcutta High Court, to whose judgment we referred earlier distinguished the English case by pointing out 
certain differences between the Corporation in that case and Hindustan Steel Limited. He pointed out that (a) in 
the English Corporation no shareholders were required to subscribe the capital or to have a voice in the affair, 
(b) the capital was raised by borrowing and not by issuance of shares, (c) the loss fell upon the consolidated 
fund and (d) the corporation was non-profit making. In our judgment these differences rather accentuate than 
diminish the applicability of the principle laid down in the English case to our case. The existence of 
shareholders, of capital raised by the issuance of shares, the lack of connection between the finances of the 
corporation and the consolidated fund of the Union rather make out a greater independent existence than that 
of the corporation in the English case. We must, therefore, hold that the corporation which is Hindustan Steel 
Limited in this case is not a department of the Government nor are the servants of it holding posts under the 
State. It has its independent existence and by law relating to Corporations it is distinct even from its members. 
In these circumstances, the appellant, who was an employee of Hindustan Steel Limited, does not answer the 
description of a holder of “a civil post under the Union” as stated in the Article. The appellant was not entitled 
to the protection of Article 311. The High Court was therefore right in not affording him the protection. The 
appeal fails and is dismissed but in the circumstances of the case we make no order about costs. 


Satinder Singh Arora v/s State Bank of Patiala & Ors., (1992) Supp (2) SCC 224, (Three Judges Bench) Held 


Held that, Bank Officers are not holders of civil posts, hence, not entitled to be protected by Article 311(1) of 
the Constitution of India. 


Basant Lal Wadehra v/s Union of India, 1996 SCC online Dethi 926, Held 


“42. The question of questions requiring consideration for resolving the above controversy is whether the peti- 
tioner was holding a 'Civil Post' at the relevant time i.e on 8.2.83 while working as Chairman-cum-Managing 
Director of Coalfields Limited (respondent No. 3). In case Lachmi v. Military Secy, to the Government of Bihar 
(AIR 1956 Pat. 398) the expression 'Civil Post' under the Union or the State was held to mean that the 'Civil 
Post’ must be in the control of the Union or the State and that it must be open to the Union or the State to 
abolish the post or to regulate the conditions of service. Patna High Court in a later case, Subodh Ranjan 
Ghosh v. Sindri Fertilisers And Chemicals Limited,, (AIR 1957 Pat. 10) held that the employees of Sindhri 
Fertilisers were not entitled to the protection of Article 311 of the Constitution. Same view has been taken by 
the High Court of Allahabad in case Ram Babu Rathaur v. Divisional Manager. Life Insurance Corporation of 
India (AIR 1961 All. 502) and by the High Court of Calcutta in case Damodar Valley Corporation v. Provat 
Roy (60 Cal. WN 1023). In case Tamlin v. Hannaford (1950-1 KB-18) it was held in relation to a business that 
although the ministry was really incharge the Corporation was different from the 'Crown' and the services of 
the 'Corporation' were not Civil Services. The Supreme Court in case Dr. S.L Aggarwal v. The General 


702 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : FEBRUARY 7, 2026/MAGHA 18, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


Manager, Hindustan Steel Limited reported as (1970) 1 SCC 177: AIR 1970 SC 1150: (1970 SLR 351 (SC)] 
held:- 


"We must, therefore, hold that the Corporation which is Hindustan Steel Limited in this case is not a depart- 
ment of the Government nor are the servants of it holding posts under the State. It has its independent exis-tence 
and by law relating to corporations it is distinct even from its members. In these circumstances, the ap-pellant, 
who was an employee of Hindustan Steel Limited, does not answer the description of a holder of व civil post 
under the Union' as stated in the Article. The appellant was not entitled to the protection of Article 311." 


43. The Supreme Court in case K.C Joshi v. Union of India reported as (1985) 3 SCC 153: AIR 1985 SC 1046: 
[1958 (2) SLR 214 (SC) observed : 


"Even if the employees of the Corporation, which is an instrumentality of the State, cannot be said to be the 
members of a civil service of the Union or an, All-India service or hold any civil post under the Union, for the 
purpose of Articles 310 and 311 and, therefore, not entitled to the protection of Article 311, they would 
nonetheless be entitled to protection of the fundamental rights enshrined in Articles 14 and 16 of the 
Constitution." 
44. In view of above cited decisions of the various High Courts and the Supreme Court, we are of the view that 
the petitioner while working as Chairman-cum-Managing Director of Coalfields Limited (respondent No. 3) 
was not holding a 'Civil Post' within the meaning of Articles 310 and 311 of the Constitution and the protection 
available to the holders of a 'Civil Post' under the provisions of Article 311 of the Constitution is, therefore, not 
available to the petitioner.” 
Though, it has been submitted by Learned Counsel for the Union that all the laws flow from Constitution of 
India and are subordinate to it. Any law, rule or regulation which is not in conformity with the Constitution is ultra- 
vires and cannot be given effect to. I am not inclined to accept this argument in the light of proposition laid down in 
the aforesaid Judgments. 


In the light of above discussion, it is held that since the employees of SECL do not hold a civil post hence, 
they are not entitled to protection of Article 311(1) of Constitution of India. 


Issue No. 1 is answered accordingly. 
Issue No. 2- 
In the light of findings on issue No. 1, this issue is answered against the Union. 
In light of above discussion and findings, the reference is answered as follows.- 
AWARD 


“Holding that the Employees and Officers of the Management of SECL do not hold Civil Post and hence 
are not entitled to protection under Article 311(1) of Constitution of India, the Delegation of Powers by the 
Management of SECL by way of Amendments in the Standing Orders is held justified in law. The actions taken by 
the Area General Managers, Sub-Area Managers and Mines Managers under the Amended Standing Orders with 
respect to disciplinary proceedings are held justified in law. The punishment orders passed by these Authorities 
under Amended Standing Orders warrant no interference.

As per letter dated 16/09/2015 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference 
has been made to this Tribunal under Section-10 of Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (in short the ‘Act’) as per 
Notification No. L-12012/97/2015(IR(B-I)) dt. 16/09/2015. The dispute under reference relates to:- 


“1. Whether Shri Manish Chatturvedi is a workman as per definition under section 2(s) of the ID Act?” 


“2. If so whether the action of the management of ICICI Bank Ltd. Indore in terminating the service of 
Shri Manish Chatturvedi ॥ 2. 27.11.2014 is justified? If not, what relief for the workman is entitled to?” 


After registering the case on the basis of reference, notices were issued to the parties. They appeared and 
filed their respective statement of claim in defense. 


The case of the workman is mainly that he was appointed w.e.f., 27.09.2010 as Assistant Manager (Band 
II) Group, RBG and joined in Gwalior. He was disengaged on 27.11.2014 without any notice or compensation or 
enquiry on the charge of self-abandonment of the job by him infact, he was suffering from spinal pain and was under 
treatment at Gwalior from 12.08.2014, he was sanctioned medical leave w.e.f., 01.07.2014 to 31.07.2014, further 
medical leave from 01.08.2014 to 20.12.2014. He further applied for medical leave w.e.f. 21.10.2014 till he attains 
fitness which was not accepted. The management issued letters dated 11.11.2014 and 21.11.2014 directing him to 
report on duty, he was not in a position to report on duty, due to his bad health and management terminated his 
services on the ground of abandonment of his service which is unjust, illegal and arbitrary. He further stated that 
though he was employed in the supervisory capacity drawing wages more than Rs. 10,000/- per month and carrying 
out the Managerial, Supervisory and Administrative functions, he has the status of workman, defined under section 
2(s) (iv) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The workman has prayed for holding aside his termination against the 
Act, he be reinstated with back wages and benefits. 


The case of the management is mainly that firstly, he is not a workman as defined under section 2(s) of 
the Act because he has been working in supervisory and managerial capacity drawing monthly pay of Rs. 38,824/- per 
month, hence, his case is not cognizable by this Tribunal. Secondly, he did not report on duty after his medical leave 
was refused on the ground of illness which he could not substantiate. Hence, taking that he has abandoned his 
services, he was terminated from service. Management has thus requested that the reference be answered against the 
workman. 


In his rejoinder the workman has mainly reiterated his allegations taken earlier. 


In evidence, the workman has filed his affidavit as his examination-in-chief, he has been cross-examined by

management. He has filed and proved documents which are his letters to Regional Labour Commissioner, letter to

dated 14.08.2014 to Dheeraj Reddy of management Bank, pay slip of April-December, 2014, three letters of

On perusal of record in light of rival arguments, following Issues came up for determination:- 


4) Whether Manish Chatturvedi, applicant is the workman as defined under section 2(s) of the Act?

Issue No.1, 


The main argument from management Bank on this issue is that the workman himself has admitted that he 
was appointed and working in managerial cadre, he was getting Rs. 38,824/- salary. He also admits that he worked in 
supervisory capacity hence, he is not a workman as defined under the Act. 


Learned Counsel for workman has submitted that only name and designation is not a determining factor for 
deciding whether the person is a workman under section 2(s) of the Act or not. 


“2(s) "Workman" means any person (including an apprentice) employed in any industry to do any 
manual, unskilled, skilled, technical, operational, clerical or supervisory work for hire or reward, 
whether the terms of employment be express or implied, and for the purposes of any proceeding 
under this Act in relation to an industrial dispute, includes any such person who has been 
dismissed, discharged or retrenched in connection with, or as a consequence of, that dispute, or 
whose dismissal, discharge or retrenchment has led to that dispute, but does not include any such 


person- 

(i) who is subject to the Air Force Act, 1950 (45 of 1950), or the Army Act, 1950 (46 of 
1950), or the Navy Act, 1957 (62 of 1957); or 

(ii) who is employed in the police service or as an officer or other employee of a prison, or 

(iii) who is employed mainly in a managerial or administrative capacity, or 

(iv) who, being employed in a supervisory capacity, draws wages exceeding ten thousand 


rupees per mensem or exercises, either by the nature of the duties attached to the office 
or by reason of the powers vested in him, functions mainly of a managerial nature.” 


Learned Counsel for Management has relied on judgment of Hon’ble High Court of Bombay in the case of 
Union Carbide (India) Ltd. V.s. Ramesh Kumbla and Others reported in MANU/MH/0073/1999 and 
another judgment of the same High Court in the case of Union Carbide (India) Ltd. V.s. D. Samuel 
and Others reported in MANU/MH/1713/1998. In these two cases, after analyzing the judgment of various 
High Courts and Hon’ble Supreme Court, the Single Bench of Hon’ble Bombay High Court has summarized 
the principles on the basis of which it is to be decided whether the Workman is in supervisory capacity or 
not. These tests mentioned in Para 34 and 35 of the Judgment are being reproduced as follows: 


Para-34. In so far as the Apex Court is concerned, some of the tests laid down are: 
(1) Designation is not material but what is important is the nature of work. 


(2) Find out the dominant purpose of employment and not any additional duties the employee 
may be performing. 


(3) Can he bind the Company/employer to some kind of decisions on behalf of the 


Company/employer. 
(4) Has the employee power to direct or oversee the work of his subordinates. 
(5) Has the power to sanction leave or recommend it; and 


(6) Has he the power to appoint, terminate or take disciplinary action against workmen.

Para-35. From the judgment of this Court and the other High Courts some of the tests apart from 
what the Apex Court has stated are: 


(a) Whether the employee can examine the quality of work and whether such work is performed in 
satisfactory manner or not; 


(b) Does the employee have powers of assigning duties and distribution of work; 

(c) Can he indent material and distribute the same amongst the workmen; 

(d) Even though he has no authority to grant leave does he have power to recommend leave; 
(e) Are there persons working under him; 

(f) Has he the power to supervise the work of men and not merely machines; 

(g) Dos he mark the attendance of other employees; 

(h) Does he write the confidential reports of his subordinates. 


Now coming to the evidence on this issue, in light of the settled proposition as referred to above, it comes 
out that in his statement of claim, the workman alleges that he was in service of the management Bank as Assistant 
Manager. He further alleges in para 4 of the statement of claim that though employed in a supervisory capacity and 
drawing Rs. 10,000/- per month also carrying out Managerial, Supervisory and Administrative functions sometimes, 
he was a workman under section 2(s) (iv) of the Act. He further pleads that the work in Bank was is of layer upon 
layers of checkers and taking his heartily supervision. He also alleges that to detect faults, assigning duties, 
distribution of works, sending reports, making arrangements for the business of the Bank with support of employees 
on contract basis does not exclude him from the category of workman under the Act. In his affidavit as his 
examination-in-chief, he states against his allegations/pleadings and states that he did not have any managerial or 
supervisory rights and used to do clerical job, he did not have any power to take disciplinary action or to punish any 
employee, he further denies in his cross-examination that employees used to report him in Ex-W/1, which has been 
filed and proved by the workman himself. He has mentioned the employees who used to report to him though, he has 
denied this document in his cross-examination but it has been filed by him only and proved by him. Hence his, this 
statement on this issue cannot be relied upon firstly, it is against his pleadings and secondly, it is against Ex-W/1 as 
referred to above. On the other hand, the management witness has corroborated this case that the workman worked in 
a supervisory and managerial capacity, hence, in light of these facts, workman is held not a workman as defined under 
section 2(s) of the Act and the issue is answered accordingly. 


Issue No. 1 is answered accordingly. 
Issue No. 2, 


The case of the workman is that he become sick and applied for leave which was sanctioned by management 
Bank up to 20.10.2014, he could not recover till date hence, again applied leave on medical grounds from 21.10.2014 
till fitness which was not accepted and he was treated absenting himself wilfully from his work place without getting

a show cause notice on 11.11.2014 and 21.11.2014 regarding his continuous unauthorized absence. These notices

condition for termination of employment when the workman had already exhausted of the leave which has accrued in

filed by the workman before the management or even before this Tribunal to show that in opinion of the doctor 
treating him, the workman was so sick that he required bed rest even after 20.10.2014. The action of management in 
terminating his services is perfectly justified in law and his terms of appointment to which he had accrued and joined 
the services of the Bank. Hence, in light of above discussion, action of management Bank in terminating the services 
of workman Manish Chatturvedi is held justified in law. 


Issue No. 2 stands answered accordingly. 

No other point was pressed.

on the basis of Pleadings and submissions of either parties, the following issues emerge for determination

2. To what relief, if any, workman is entitled to? 


Finding 
Issue No. I:- 


Petitioner has alleged that he was appointed as a casual messenger in April 1996 on payment of Rs. 20 per 
day and had worked continuously without any break to the entire satisfaction of the superior officer. Further, it is 
alleged that Petitioner has terminated from service by the Respondent vide order dated 27" June 2013, without 
conducting an inquiry, notice pay, and compensation, in violation of provisions contained under sections 25F, 25G, 
and 25H of the Industrial Disputes Act. on the other hand, Respondent has denied the allegation and contended that 
the petitioner was engaged as a casual labour by the Respondent to meet exigencies of the work, and soon after the 
exigencies are met, the term of casual labour automatically would also come to an end. Therefore, same cannot be 
described as a termination of service by the Respondent. It is undisputed that the petitioner had worked in the 
Respondent branch as a casual labour on a daily wages basis. Now, we would examine the legality of the termination 
of the petitioner from service by the Respondent. 


In this regard, the relevant provisions contained under section 25F of the ID Act are extracted as here under:- 


25-F. Conditions precedent to retrenchment of workmen:-No workman employed in any industry who has been in 
continuous service for not less than one year under an employer shall be retrenched by that employer until- 


(a) the workman has been given one month's notice in writing indicating the reasons for retrenchment and the 
period of notice has expired, or the workman has been paid in lieu of such notice, wages for the period of the 
notice. 


[xxx] 


(b) the workman has been paid, at the time of retrenchment, compensation which shall be equivalent to fifteen days' 
average pay [for every completed year of continuous service] or any part thereof in excess of six months; and 


(c) notice in the prescribed manner is served on the appropriate Government [or such authority as may be specified by 
the appropriate Government by notification in the Official Gazette]. 


As per provision, contained the 25F, the condition precedent for retrenchment is that the petitioner had 
worked for 240 days continuously in a 12-month just preceding the date of his termination, and burden of proof lies 
upon the shoulders of the petitioner to prove this fact. In support of his allegation, the petitioner has examined himself 
as WWI, and in chief statement affidavit, the petitioner has stated that he was appointed as casual messenger on 
April 1996 in the Respondent bank branch and had worked continuously without any break to the entire satisfaction 
of the superior officers, and he has been terminated from service by the Respondent by vide order dated 27" June 
2013. This witness was cross-examined by the Respondent's counsel, and in his cross-examination, WW1 has stated 
that he joined in the Respondent bank on a daily wage basis, and for the first two years, he was paid weekly. Further, 
witness State WWI states that he was regularly employed but was not issued any appointment letter from the 
Respondent bank. WW1 states that he used to allotted work on a daily basis and used to file the vouchers. Further, 
witness WW1 state that initially, he was getting wages in the form of cash, and he used to get pay slips for the wages 
drawn by him. He has filed the pay slip. The document filed by the petitioner are: Exhibit W1 is the copy of the 
termination order, which goes reveals that the petitioner, D. Ramarao, was engaged as a casual labour, and the 
competent authority has decided to discontinue his services as a casual labour with immediate effect vide letter dated 
27" June, 2013. Furthermore, Ex: W4 to W8 are the particulars of wages paid to the petitioner, which goes show that 
petitioner, workman, has been paid wages in month of January 2013, February 2013, March 2013, April 2013, and 
May 2013 for the work of number of days in the Respondent branch. Further, the documentary evidence filed by the 
petitioner would not depicts that he has worked for 240 days continuously in the Respondent branch just preceding 
from the date of his termination, i.e., 277 June 2013. Thus, petitioner has failed to discharge the burden of proof 
regarding 240 days of continuous service just preceding the date of his termination. Whereas Respondent has 
examined witness MW1 in support of his contention, who has categorically in his chief statement stated that petitioner 
was engaged as a casual labour by the Respondents, and the petitioner is well aware of the fact that the engagement is 
not permanent. Therefore, there is no permanency of the service, and hence the question of termination of the 
petitioner's service by the Respondent does not arise. Further, witness MW 1 states that as soon as the exigency of the 
work is completed, the person engaged for the purpose of such work would naturally become redundant. Hence, the 
engagement of such a person is for a specific purpose, and the person so engaged cannot claim either continuity or

permanency or treatment on par of with the regular employees. Further, this witness, MW1, was cross-examined by 
the petitioner counsel, but nothing has been rightly stated in the cross-examination to discredit the testimony of the 
witness MW1. Further, the Respondent has relied upon the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Himanshu 
Kumar Vidyarthi Vs State of Bihar, date of decision 26" March 1997, wherein the Honourable Supreme Court held 
that daily wagers have no right to post, and their disengagement is not arbitrary. Since they are temporary employees 
working on daily wages, their engagement from service cannot be treated under Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. 


Thus, in view of the above, the petitioner has failed to discharge his burden of proof that he has been 
retrenched in contravention of the provisions contained in Section 25(f) of the ID Act. As regards the burden of proof, 
certain decisions of the Honourable Supreme Court are Relevant are regarding Burden of Proof In case of 
Retrenchment, which are being discussed as hereunder: - 


(a).Further, in Rajasthan State Ganganagar S. Mills Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan and Anr. (2004) Apex Court held: 


"It was the case of the workman that he had worked for more than 240 days in the year concerned. This 
claim was denied by the appellant. It was for the claimant to lead evidence to show that he had worked for 240 days in 
the year preceding the date of his termination. He has filed an affidavit. It is statement which is in his favor and that 
cannot be regarded as sufficient evidence for any Court or Tribunal to come to the conclusion that in fact the claimant 
had worked for 240 days in a year." 


(b).In the case of Mohan Lal v. Management, BEL 1981 SCC P. 225. Hon'ble Apex Court held:- 


“Before a workman can claim retrenchment, not being in consonance of Section 25 of the ID act he has to 
show that he has been in continuous service of not less than 1 year with the employer who had retrenched him from 
service The Hon'ble Apex Court in this case also laid down the principle of how to count 240 days of service within 
one year and held: "Clause (2)(a) provides for a fiction to treat a workman in continuous service for a period of one 
year despite the fact that he has not rendered uninterrupted service for a period of one year but he has rendered service 
period of 240 days during the period of 12 calendar months for counting backwards and just preceding the relevant 
date being the date of retrenchment. In other words, in order to invoke the fiction enacted in clause (2)(a) it is 
necessary to determine first the relevant date, ie the date of termination of service which is complained of as 
retrenchment. After that date is ascertained move backward to a period of 12 months just preceding the date of 
retrenchment and then ascertain whether within the period of 12 months, the workman has rendered service for a 
period of 240 days. If these three facts are affirmatively answered in favor of the workman pursuant to the deeming 
fiction enacted in clause (2)(a) it will have to be assumed that the workman is in continuous service for a period of 
one year and he will satisfy the eligibility qualification enacted in Section 25-77 


(c).In the case of GM., BSNL and others V. Mahesh Chand AIR 2008 SC (Supp) 1328, wherein the Hon'ble Apex 
Court have held, 


"It was the case of the claimant that he had so worked but this claim was denied by the appellant. It was then 
for the claimant to lead evidence to show that he had in fact worked for 240 days in the year preceding his 
termination. Filing of an affidavit is only his own statement in his favour and that cannot be regarded as 
sufficient evidence forany Court or Tribunal to come to the conclusion that a workman had, in fact, worked for 240 
days in a year. No proof of receipt of salary or wages for 240 days or order or record of appointment or engagement 
for this period was produced by the workman. On this ground alone, the award is liable to be set aside." 


(d). In the case of Range Forest Officer Vs. S T Hadimani AIR 2002 SC page 1147, wherein Hon'ble Apex Court 
have held, 


"the onus lies upon claimant to show that he had in fact worked for 240 days in a year-In absence of proof of 
receipt of salary or wages record of appointment, filing of an affidavit by workman is not sufficient evidence to prove 
that he had worked for 240 days in a year preceding his termination.” 


(e). In the case of Essen Deinki Vs. Rajiv Kumar, AIR 2003 SC 38 the Hon'ble Apex Court have held, 


"It was for the employee concerned to prove that he has in fact completed 240 days in the last preceding 12 
months’ period." 


(f). In the case of Municipal Corporation, Faridabad Vs. Siri Niwas AIR 2004 SC 4681, wherein Hon'ble Apex Court 
have held:- 


"that the burden of proof was on the workman to show that he had worked for 240 days in the preceding 12 
months prior to his alleged retrenchment u/s 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. It is also held that it is 
improbable that a person working in a Local Authority would not be in possession of any documentary evidence to 
support his claim before the tr. Apart from muster rolls he could have shown the terms and conditions of his offer of 
appointment and the remuneration received by him for working during the afore mentioned period. He even did not 
examine any other witness in support of his case." 


(g). In the case of Chief Engineer, Ranjit Sagar Dam and another Vs. Sham Lal, 2006 AIR SCW 3574, wherein the

Hon'ble Apex Court have held: 


"Fact that workman had worked for 240 days or more in year immediately preceding termination Burden of proof 
Burden is on workman not on employer-delay of nine years in seeking-no relief could be given to claimant." 
Manager, RBI, Bangalore vs. S. Mani & Ors., on 14.3.2005 AIR 2005 Supreme Court 2179 have held that, merely the 
completion of 240 days of continuous service by the workmen by itself does not give rise to claim of permanence in 
the employment Hon'ble Supreme Court have held that:- 


"It may not be out of place to mention that completion of 240 days of continuous service in a year may not 
by itself be a ground for directing an order of regularization. It is also not the case of the Respondents that they were 
appointed in accordance with the extant rules. No direction for regularization of their services was, therefore, 
could be issued." 


Therefore, in view of the foregoing discussion and law laid down by the Honourable court as discussed 
above, I am of the considered opinion that the Petitioner has failed to establish that his services have been terminated 
by the Respondent in contravention of provision of section 25F, 25G,25H of the Act. Thus, the issue is decided 
against the petitioner. 

Issue No. II:- 

In view of the foregone discussion and finding given at Issue No. I, the action of the Respondent 
management has been found legal and justified. Therefore, the action of the Respondent management in terminating 
the services of the petitioner has been found legal and justified. Therefore, petitioner is not entitled to any relief, and 
petition is deserved to be dismissed. 

AWARD 


In view of findings given at Issue No. I and II, the action of Respondent management in terminating the 
services of petitioner, vide order dated 27-06-2013 is held legal and justified. The Petitioner devoid of merit hence 
stands dismissed. Reference is answered accordingly.

Kumar Vidyarthi Vs State of Bihar, date of decision 26" March 1997, wherein the Honourable Supreme Court held 
that daily wagers have no right to post, and their disengagement is not arbitrary. Since they are temporary employees 
working on daily wages, their engagement from service cannot be treated under Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. 


Thus, in view of the above, the petitioner has failed to discharge his burden of proof that he has been 


[भाग ए---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : फरवरी 7, 2026/माध 18, 1947 715 


retrenched in contravention of the provisions contained in Section 250) of the ID Act. As regards the burden of proof, 
certain decisions of the Honourable Supreme Court are Relevant regarding Burden of Proof In case of Retrenchment, 
of workman which are being discussed as hereunder: - 


(a). In Rajasthan State Ganganagar S. Mills Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan and Anr. (2004) Apex Court held: 


"It was the case of the workman that he had worked for more than 240 days in the year concerned. This 
claim was denied by the appellant. It was for the claimant to lead evidence to show that he had worked for 240 days in 
the year preceding the date of his termination. He has filed an affidavit. It is statement which is in his favor and that 
cannot be regarded as sufficient evidence for any Court or Tribunal to come to the conclusion that in fact the claimant 
had worked for 240 days in a year." 


(b).In the case of Mohan Lal v. Management, BEL 1981 SCC P. 225. Hon'ble Apex Court held:- 


“Before a workman can claim retrenchment, not being in consonance of Section 25 of the ID act he has to 
show that he has been in continuous service of not less than 1 year with the employer who had retrenched him from 
service The Hon'ble Apex Court in this case also laid down the principle of how to count 240 days of service within 
one year and held: "Clause (2)(a) provides for a fiction to treat a workman in continuous service for a period of one 
year despite the fact that he has not rendered uninterrupted service for a period of one year but he has rendered service 
period of 240 days during the period of 12 calendar months for counting backwards and just preceding the relevant 
date being the date of retrenchment. In other words, in order to invoke the fiction enacted in clause (2)(a) it is 
necessary to determine first the relevant date, ie the date of termination of service which is complained of as 
retrenchment. After that date is ascertained move backward to a period of 12 months just preceding the date of 
retrenchment and then ascertain whether within the period of 12 months, the workman has rendered service for a 
period of 240 days. If these three facts are affirmatively answered in favor of the workman pursuant to the deeming 
fiction enacted in clause (2)(a) it will have to be assumed that the workman is in continuous service for a period of 
one year and he will satisfy the eligibility qualification enacted in Section 25-F”’ 


(c).In the case of GM., BSNL and others V. Mahesh Chand AIR 2008 SC (Supp) 1328, wherein the Hon'ble Apex 
Court have held, 


"It was the case of the claimant that he had so worked but this claim was denied by the appellant. It was then 
for the claimant to lead evidence to show that he had in fact worked for 240 days in the year preceding his 
termination. Filing of an affidavit is only his own statement in his favour and that cannot be regarded as 
sufficient evidence forany Court or Tribunal to come to the conclusion that a workman had, in fact, worked for 240 
days in a year. No proof of receipt of salary or wages for 240 days or order or record of appointment or engagement 
for this period was produced by the workman. On this ground alone, the award is liable to be set aside." 


(d). In the case of Range Forest Officer Vs. S T Hadimani AIR 2002 SC page 1147, wherein Hon'ble Apex Court 
have held, 


"the onus lies upon claimant to show that he had in fact worked for 240 days in a year-In absence of proof of 
receipt of salary or wages record of appointment, filing of an affidavit by workman is not sufficient evidence to prove 
that he had worked for 240 days in a year preceding his termination.” 


(e). In the case of Essen Deinki Vs. Rajiv Kumar, AIR 2003 SC 38 the Hon'ble Apex Court have held, 


"It was for the employee concerned to prove that he has in fact completed 240 days in the last preceding 12 
months’ period." 


(f). In the case of Municipal Corporation, Faridabad Vs. Siri Niwas AIR 2004 SC 4681, wherein Hon'ble Apex Court 
have held:- 


"that the burden of proof was on the workman to show that he had worked for 240 days in the preceding 12 
months prior to his alleged retrenchment u/s 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. It is also held that it is 
improbable that a person working in a Local Authority would not be in possession of any documentary evidence to 
support his claim before the tr. Apart from muster rolls he could have shown the terms and conditions of his offer of 
appointment and the remuneration received by him for working during the afore mentioned period. He even did not 
examine any other witness in support of his case." 


(g). In the case of Chief Engineer, Ranjit Sagar Dam and another Vs. Sham Lal, 2006 AIR SCW 3574, wherein the 
Hon'ble Apex Court have held: 


"Fact that workman had worked for 240 days or more in year immediately preceding termination Burden of proof 
Burden is on workman not on employer-delay of nine years in seeking-no relief could be given to claimant." 
Manager, RBI, Bangalore vs. S. Mani & Ors., on 14.3.2005 AIR 2005 Supreme Court 2179 have held that, merely the 
completion of 240 days of continuous service by the workmen by itself does not give rise to claim of permanence in 
the employment Hon'ble Supreme Court have held that:- 


716 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : FEBRUARY 7, 2026/MAGHA 18, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


"It may not be out of place to mention that completion of 240 days of continuous service in a year may not 
by itself be a ground for directing an order of regularization. It is also not the case of the Respondents that they were 
appointed in accordance with the extant rules. No direction for regularization of their services was, therefore, 
could be issued." 


Therefore, in view of the foregoing discussion and law laid down by the Honourable court as discussed 
above, I am of the considered opinion that the Petitioner has failed to establish that his services have been terminated 
by the Respondent in contravention of provision of section 25F, 25G,25H of the Act. Thus, this issue is decided 
against the petitioner. 


Issue No. II:- 


In view of the foregone discussion and finding given at Issue No. I, Petitioner failed to establish that 
Respondent management has terminated him services illegally. Therefore, the action of the Respondent management 
in terminating the services of the petitioner held legal and justified. Therefore, petitioner has not entitled to any relief, 
and petition deserved to be dismissed. 


AWARD 


In view of findings given at Issue No. I and I, the action of Respondent management in terminating the 
services of petitioner, B. Govinda Raju vide order dated 10-07-2013 is held legal and justified. The Petition is devoid 
of merit hence stands dismissed. Reference is answered accordingly.

ORDER
